opus-5.5.text:
I think right now data is the bigger bottleneck, by a wide margin. If you look at what happened in language models, the architecture, the Transformer, has been fairly stable for years. Most of the progress came from scaling up data and compute, and from getting smarter about data quality and the training recipe. In robotics we're in a very different place: we simply don't have an internet-scale corpus of robot interaction data. Every trajectory has to be collected on a physical robot, often through teleoperation, and that's slow and expensive. So when I talk to my team, I usually say: if you have a fixed amount of effort, putting it into getting more and better data will almost always pay off more than tweaking the architecture.

That said, I don't think architecture is unimportant. Some architectural choices really matter in robotics because the problem is different from text. You have high-frequency continuous control, multiple camera views, proprioception, sometimes touch, and you need to run in real time on a robot. So things like how you represent actions, whether you use diffusion or flow matching for action generation, how you combine a big vision-language backbone with a fast low-level controller: those are real design decisions, and getting them wrong can hurt a lot. But I see them as enabling choices. They let you absorb data efficiently and run reliably; they're not the thing that suddenly gives you general intelligence.

The other point is that architecture and data aren't fully separate. A good architecture lets you use more kinds of data. For example, if your model can learn from human videos, from simulation, from different robot embodiments, then you've effectively enlarged your dataset. That's where I think the most interesting architecture work is: not squeezing an extra few percent on a benchmark, but making the model able to learn from heterogeneous, messy sources so that data stops being so scarce.

So my short answer: data first, and architecture in service of data. The field will look back and see that the breakthroughs came when we figured out how to scale data, whether through cheaper collection, simulation, or learning from humans, and the architecture just needed to be good enough to soak it all up.

r001.rationale: The response identifies data as robotics’ bigger bottleneck and says architecture serves data rather than providing general intelligence on its own. It also explains that architecture can help models use more data, supporting the point that architectural innovation cannot make up for insufficient data.

fable-5.1.text:
Honestly, I think architecture matters much less than people assume, and data matters much more. If you look back at the history of robot learning, the big jumps rarely came from a clever new network design. They came from someone finally getting enough of the right data into a reasonably standard model.

I say that as someone who spent years on the architecture side. Early on in legged locomotion we tried all kinds of specialized structures, hierarchical controllers, hand-designed inductive biases. Almost all of it got washed away once we could run large-scale simulation and train on billions of samples. A plain MLP with good data beat the fancy architecture with little data, every time.

That said, I would not say architecture is irrelevant. It matters in a specific way, which is that it determines whether you can absorb the data you have. The transformer did not win because it was elegant, it won because it scales gracefully with data and compute. In robotics the analogous question is how you represent actions, how you handle multiple modalities, how you deal with different embodiments. Those are architecture questions, but they are really in service of data, they are about making heterogeneous robot data usable at all.

So my view is that data is the bottleneck, and architecture innovation is valuable when it unlocks more data or makes existing data more effective. Architecture innovation for its own sake, chasing a point or two on a benchmark, I am fairly skeptical of. In robotics the real problem is that we simply do not have the internet-scale corpus that language and vision had. Whether that comes from simulation, from teleoperation, from human video, from fleets of deployed robots, solving that supply problem is what will determine progress over the next few years, far more than any single model design.

r001.rationale: The response says a plain model with good data outperformed fancy architectures with little data, and identifies data supply as robotics’ bottleneck, conveying that architecture cannot make up for insufficient data.

astra-6.text:
I think architecture innovation is important, but it has to go hand in hand with data. A better architecture can help a robot learn more efficiently and incorporate useful structure, but it can’t fully compensate for a lack of diverse experience.

In robotics, collecting that experience is particularly challenging. You have to interact with the physical world, and that takes time and introduces hardware and safety constraints. So I would put a lot of emphasis on building a scalable way to collect good data, alongside developing better models.

I also wouldn’t say that once we have enough data, architecture stops mattering. The two reinforce each other. The key question is which one is the bottleneck for the capability you’re trying to achieve.

r001.rationale: The response says a better architecture “can’t fully compensate for a lack of diverse experience,” conveying that architectural innovation cannot make up for insufficient data coverage in robotics.

sol-6.1.text:
I think architecture innovation is important, but sufficient data is often the more fundamental bottleneck in robotics. If you have a small dataset, it’s hard to tell whether a new architecture is really better or whether it just fits that particular dataset better. With large, diverse datasets, you can make that comparison much more reliably.

That doesn’t mean architecture doesn’t matter. A good architecture can help a robot learn more efficiently and generalize to new situations. But I wouldn’t expect architecture alone to compensate for a lack of experience. In robotics, we need to invest heavily in collecting useful data and building a process where the robot’s failures help us decide what data to collect next. Architecture and data should improve together.

r001.rationale: The candidate says architecture alone cannot compensate for a lack of experience and emphasizes the need for large, diverse robotics datasets, covering insufficient data volume and coverage.
